title: Frutiger typeface
lede: Adrian Frutiger’s humanist sans-serif for airport signs, and the other half of the style’s name.
summary: Open, legible humanist sans-serif. Adrian Frutiger, released 1976.
made: 1976 (public release by Stempel with Linotype; developed from the Roissy signage type of 1970/71)

evidence.note: Inspected the public-domain specimen [File:FrutigerSpec-1.svg](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:FrutigerSpec-1.svg), rendered by Wikimedia at 960 px wide, and stored it.

styles.note: The style is named partly after this typeface; its open humanist forms match the friendly type of the period, though the typeface itself was not the Aero interface font.

context: Frutiger is a humanist sans-serif by Adrian Frutiger. It is the text version of Roissy, commissioned in 1970/71 for the signs of Charles de Gaulle Airport, and was released publicly in 1976 by Stempel with Linotype. [Wikipedia: Frutiger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frutiger_(typeface)).

CARI says the name joins Vista’s “Aero” guideline with Frutiger’s typeface, “which originally inspired Vista’s default font (Segoe UI).” [CARI: Frutiger Aero](https://cari.institute/aesthetics/frutiger-aero).

Avcı notes that Frutiger “was not used in the Aero, TouchWiz, or MacOS X interfaces associated with the movement,” so the name can mislead. [Avcı 2024, “Physical reflections of digital aesthetics”](https://doi.org/10.17932/IAU.EJNM.25480200.2024/ejnm_v8i3003), pp. 463–464. See [Segoe UI](ref:segoe-ui-typeface).
observed: Letters are open and round with wide apertures: the a, e, and c curl in only slightly.
The a is double-storey; the g is single-storey; the i has a square dot.
The large lowercase x-height makes the specimen’s lowercase nearly as tall as the capitals.
The specimen shows the airport phrase “Accès aux avions” in gray.
interpretation: The link to the style is typological, not literal: the era’s interfaces used humanist sans-serifs with the same openness and warmth, and Frutiger stands for that family in the name.
borrow: Pair glossy surfaces with an open humanist sans-serif, not a geometric or grotesque one. The warmth of the letters carries the “friendly technology” tone.

images.alt: Type specimen of Frutiger: the name in bold, “Aa Ee Rr” in regular and bold, a large white lowercase a, “Accès aux avions” in gray, and the lowercase alphabet and figures on a yellow band.
